candidate.answerReason: Positivity of the outer logarithm's argument successively requires the inner values to exceed 1 and 2002, giving exactly \(x>2001^{2002}\). The boundary makes the outer argument zero and is excluded.

methods.label: Work inward from the outer logarithm
methods.explanation:
A real logarithm is defined exactly when its argument is positive. For an admissible input, write the three inner values as
\[
u=\log_{2001}x,\qquad
v=\log_{2002}u,\qquad
w=\log_{2003}v.
\]
The outermost logarithm is \(\log_{2004}w\), so it requires \(w>0\).

All the bases exceed 1, so these logarithmic functions are increasing. Using \(\log_a1=0\) and \(\log_aa=1\), the requirements work inward as follows:
\[
\begin{aligned}
w>0&\Longleftrightarrow v>1,\\
v>1&\Longleftrightarrow u>2002,\\
u>2002&\Longleftrightarrow x>2001^{2002}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Conversely, if \(x>2001^{2002}\), then \(x>0\), \(u>2002>0\), \(v>1>0\), and \(w>0\). Thus every logarithm has a positive argument, proving that this condition is sufficient as well as necessary.

At \(x=2001^{2002}\), the inner values are \(u=2002\), \(v=1\), and \(w=0\), so the outermost logarithm is undefined. Hence the domain is exactly \(x>2001^{2002}\), and
\[
c=\boxed{2001^{2002}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
